newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says Archer tax plan violates budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Archer tax plan violates budget pact.

text.p: President Clinton said Tuesday a new Republican tax cut plan violated the balanced budget deal reached last month, was unfair to middle class families and shortchanged his educational proposals.

Making his first public comments on the programme unveiled Monday by Representative Bill Archer, Republican chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee that writes tax legislation, Clinton said he hoped Congress would work with him to revise the plan.
Archer laid out his vision for a five-year, $85 billion tax cut plan that provides the detail to the overall balanced budget accord reached May 2 by Clinton and the Republicans who control Congress.
But Clinton, speaking at an unrelated White House event on educational standards, argued that Archer's programme violated that agreement in several respects.
"I have reviewed this plan and I believe that in its present form it does not meet the tests that I would hold myself to," Clinton said, listing the tests as the following:

"One, being faithful to the budget agreement; second, having a tax cut that will grow the economy; third, having a tax cut that is fair to middle class families; and, fourth, having a tax cut that genuinely helps to increase the quality and volume of education in America."
He added: "I hope that the House Democrats and Republicans and the Senate Democrats and Republicans will work with us to meet those tests."

Clinton's comments, which followed criticism by top U.S. officials Monday, showed that the White House wants to do everything it can to rework the tax programme, although under the balanced budget deal it left writing the details of the tax proposals to the congressional committees.

Clinton said Archer's plan violated that pact by reducing the overall tax cuts for higher education, falling $13 billion short of the $35 billion laid out in the agreement. "We agreed to roughly $35 billion. You might say that $34 billion is roughly $35 billion, but $22 billion is not," he said.
By Archer's count, the education-related tax cuts amount to $31 billion.
The president also criticised Archer's treatment of his "Hope Scholarships" proposal, under which Clinton had proposed a $1,500 tax credit to defray the costs of higher education.
Archer's proposal would give a 50 percent tax credit for higher education expenses of up to $3,000, which Clinton said would reduce the benefit for those attending cheaper colleges.

"Those who intend to go to less expensive schools like community colleges would have the Hope scholarship I proposed (and) specifically agreed to in the budget agreement, cut in half by the House plan," he said.

According to an administration official, the budget pact called for $35 billion in tax cuts for the Hope Scholarships programme and a related $10,000 education tax deduction but, as drafted by Archer, this came to only $22 billion.

The official said Archer's plan provides a further $9 billion for other education-related tax cuts, bringing his total to $31 billion, but the White House believes these should not count toward the $35 billion under the pact.
Clinton also sharply criticised the Archer plan's treatment of the proposed child tax credit, which would be $400 in the next fiscal year, rising to $500 thereafter.

Clinton said the credit would discriminate againt lower income citizens because it would be computed after the earned income tax credit for the working poor and after a credit for child care expenses of families where both parents work.

"In short, the tax plan cuts in half the tax cuts for those who go to community college. It shortchanges 6 million families who are already in the work force and having to pay for their child care," he said. "That does not meet the standards of fairness and promotion of education."
